title: Early and late leaf spot of groundnut

Header: Early and late leaf spot of groundnut

Prevention: Collect old plant debris from the field immediately after harvest and burn or bury to reduce inoculum levels for the next season crop
Plant early when disease pressure is low
Crop rotation with any other crop for at least 2 years to reduce inoculum levels of early and late leaf spot pathogens
Intercrop with millet, maize, cotton, sorghum and soy bean to reduce spread of spores
Regularly weed the fields to reduce humidity within groundnut crops, thus preventing infection
Monitoring: Early and late leaf spot are caused by different fungi and can be difficult to tell apart and a single plant can have both diseases at the same time
Inspect field at least once a week looking for symptoms:
Early leaf spot: light brown spots with a yellow margin and rough silvery, hair- like spores can be seen on the upper surface of infected leaf
Late leaf spot: look for dark brown/ black circular spots (darker than early leaf spot).
Spores are formed on the lower side of the leaves.
The spores are arranged in circular rings and have a rough appearance
Lesions may develop on stem petioles and pegs.
In severe infections, the leaves or pods may fall off
Apply direct control as soon as leaf spots are seen.
Direct Control: Remove infected plants when disease incidence is low, then bury or burn to reduce the spread or reinfection of healthy plants
Carbendazim 50WP, Goldazim 500SC) at 1.5-2.0ml/L of water 30 days after sowing if signs of leaf spot outbreak persist.
Agrithane 80WP, Benco 80WP, Damazeb 80WP, Dizcozeb 80WP etc.) at a rate of 5g/L of water 30 days after sowing if signs of leaf spot outbreak persist.
Multi- site broad spectrum contact fungicide.
